Transform LASA data between long and wide format

Source: R/lasa_transform.R
transform_lasa_data.Rd

Reshapes LASA data between wide format – one row per respondent, with a separate column for each variable at each wave (boak, coak, doak, ...), the way LASA's Z files (e.g. LASAZOA1.SAV) store information that spans waves – and long format: one row per respondent per wave, one column per variable (oak), and a "Wave" column saying which wave each row belongs to, the way read_lasa_sav() returns a single wave file. Works on a file read by read_lasa_sav() (read_lasa_sav(format_as_long = TRUE) calls it for you), on several LASA files merged together, and on any data frame with a respnr column.

Usage

transform_lasa_data(data, format = "long", prefix = "Wave")

Arguments

data

A data frame or tibble with one respondent identifier column named respnr (in any capitalization), for example the result of read_lasa_sav(), or several LASA files merged together. Long data also have a "Wave" column (in any capitalization) of LASA wave codes.

format

"long" (the default) or "wide": the format to transform data into.

prefix

"Wave" (the default) or "Time": what the names of wave-specific columns start with in wide format. Only used when format = "wide"; see Details.

Value

data in the requested format, as a data frame (or a tibble if data is one), keeping data's provenance attributes. Its "LASA_wave" attribute is updated to the data's single wave if there is only one, removed from long data that span several waves, and "Z" for wide data that span several waves (as for a Z file). Long data that span several waves can't be relabelled with apply_lasa_labels(), which labels one file and wave at a time: label each file before transforming it.

Details

Long format has one row per respondent per wave, with a "Wave" column (the LASA wave code, e.g. "B", "2B", "MB") and a "Time" column right after respnr. Each wave-specific variable becomes one column named after its wave-stripped (canonical) name, so boak, coak, ... become oak. A respondent gets a row for each wave at which at least one of the wave-specific columns has a value for them – anything but NA or blank text (which is how SPSS stores missing text), so a missing-value code kept as a value (read with read_lasa_sav(keep_user_na = TRUE)) counts too. Respondents of a later cohort therefore only get rows for the waves before they joined LASA where the data hold such a code for them, as LASA's Z files do ("no observation birth cohorts 1938-1947"). A respondent without any value at any wave keeps a row for every wave, so nobody disappears. Rows are sorted by respondent (in order of first appearance) and wave, except in long data without wide columns, which keep their order.

Time counts the waves since the respondent's baseline, the wave at which their cohort joined LASA, which is Time 0. A cohort takes part in every later wave except the other cohorts' baselines:

  • first cohort: B = 0, C = 1, D = 2, E = 3, F = 4, G = 5, H = 6, I = 7, J = 8, K = 9, L = 10;

  • second cohort: 2B = 0, F = 1, G = 2, H = 3, I = 4, J = 5, K = 6, L = 7;

  • third cohort and migrant cohort: 3B or MB = 0, I = 1, J = 2, K = 3, L = 4;

  • fourth cohort: 4B = 0, L = 1.

Wave A, the LSN pilot study a few months before wave B, isn't part of any cohort's waves: its rows keep "Wave" "A" and have no Time (NA). Time counts waves, not years, and it isn't LASA's own wave numbering, which LASAZ008.SAV uses (t2_dat is wave B there); for time itself, use the interview dates or ages in LASAZ008.SAV.

A row's Time depends on the respondent's cohort, which the data show by:

  • a value (other than NA, blank text, or a missing-value code) at the respondent's baseline or at a wave only their cohort takes part in (B to E for the first cohort);

  • a single LASA file of such a wave, whose respondents all belong to its cohort, whatever their values (the data's "LASA_file_code" and "LASA_wave" attributes say which file; not a Z file, whose rows may hold codes for waves before a cohort joined): in long data all of whose rows are of that wave, any row, unless it holds nothing but values a guess put at its wave (see Names of several waves); in wide data (the file read with LASA's own names, standardize = FALSE in read_lasa_sav(), or transformed to wide format), every respondent, as long as all columns are the file's (those its label report lists, and the names wide format gives columns of its wave) – once other data are joined on, every respondent with a value in one of the file's columns (one the join added has none), also when the file in wide data was joined onto long data, keeping its attributes (as dplyr's joins do with it first);

  • LASA's cohort column, as LASAZ002.SAV and Time-prefixed wide data (see Wide format) have it: "cohort 1 (1992)" – also written "Cohort 1" or "cohort 1 (1992/1993)" – or its code 1 is the first cohort, whose baseline is B; cohort 2's is 2B, cohort 3's 3B, cohort 4's 4B, and the "migrant cohort"'s MB;

  • a "Time" column already in long data;

  • the respondent number: LASA numbers its respondents with five digits, the first of which is 1, 2, or 3 in the first cohort, 4, 5, or 6 in the second cohort, and 7, 8, or 9 in the third. A 1 also numbers the LSN pilot study's respondents, so it only says the first cohort of a respondent the data show at a wave other than A, by a value there (rows that hold nothing but missing-value codes don't count). The fourth and the migrant cohort's numbers aren't known yet: if they have five digits too, they say one of the first three cohorts until the rest of the data show their own (their baseline file, say, or a cohort column). A number of any other form (the longer numbers the fourth cohort may have, or the small numbers of the examples below) says nothing. Where the rest of the data show another cohort than a respondent's number, they decide, with a warning in long and Time-prefixed wide format, which show the cohort – also over a "Time" column that follows the number, as read_lasa_sav() and long format give it where the data don't show the cohort: at waves several cohorts share, and on rows holding nothing but missing-value codes (a Time at wave B is the first cohort's). Such a Time gives way also where a file of a wave of one cohort gave it, which stacked files no longer show.

A missing-value code is what read_lasa_sav() turns into NA unless keep_user_na = TRUE: an SPSS user-missing value; in a variable the label database documents, any negative code, documented or not, except in a variable whose values can be negative at that wave (such as the speech-reception thresholds msrttn), where only its documented codes are; and in any column, a negative code with a value label – also as the text or factor level read_lasa_sav() gives it (its label, or its own number). Values show the cohort in the wave-specific variables the label database documents (and long columns transform_lasa_data() made from wide columns); in long data without any, in the columns whose values differ between a respondent's rows (a variable computed per wave, say; an NA counts as a value of its own), or else in all columns but the documented stable variables; and in long data without such columns, every row shows its wave. The waves from F on, which cohorts share, don't show the cohort: the rows of a respondent seen only at those waves get no Time, with a message, unless their respondent number or another of the sources above shows it (or every cohort the data leave open gives their wave the same Time). Data showing waves of several cohorts for one respondent give that respondent no Time, with a warning.

A "Time" column already in long data – also the Time.x/Time.y columns merge() makes of two, and the further copies merging more data sets gives (Time.x.x, or several of the same name) – must give each row a Time that the respondent's cohort, as far as the rest of the data show it, gives its wave, and copies must agree with each other, except that a copy following the respondent number gives way to one that doesn't (that of a file of a wave several cohorts share read on its own, next to that of data that showed another cohort, say); it is replaced by the recomputed one.

A cohort column (in any capitalization) is LASA's when its values, factor levels, or value labels name cohorts the way above, or when it holds nothing but their codes (and missing values): LASA's codes 1 to 4, and 5 for the migrant cohort, as Time-prefixed wide data code it, as numbers, or as text or factor levels ("4", the way read_lasa_sav() reads a code the label database doesn't document) – unless value labels say they are something else (birth cohorts, say; labels of negative missing-value codes aside). In a column whose value labels name cohorts, a code without a value label names its cohort too, as does one labelled with its own number (the level "4" in a .sav file). Any other cohort column is an ordinary column. LASA's cohort column must give each respondent one cohort, which the waves the data show must fit; values that name no cohort (a missing-value code) say nothing. In long format, it stays as it is; coded as Time-prefixed wide data have it (as read_lasa_sav() reads LASAZ002.SAV's), it gets back the labels merge() and row subsetting drop. Several columns named cohort – the cohort.x/cohort.y columns of data sets with a cohort column merged by respnr (LASAZ002.SAV, Time-prefixed wide data), the further copies merging more of them gives (cohort.x.x, or several of the same name), and columns whose names differ in capitalization only (LASAZ002.SAV's COHORT as haven::read_sav() reads it, next to Time-prefixed wide data's cohort) – are combined into one cohort, coded as Time-prefixed wide data have it, and must agree. A copy that names no cohort is another data set's own column, and stays as it is; a column named cohort that names none, next to one that does, is an error.

Stable variables – columns that hold for every wave, such as sex or year of birth (byear) in LASAZ004.SAV – keep one column and are repeated on each of the respondent's rows: in long data, a stable variable the label database documents is filled in on the respondent's rows where it is missing (rows other files' columns added, or rows of other waves merged in by respnr and "Wave") from their other rows, as long as those agree. A file without wave-specific columns, such as LASAZ004.SAV or the migrant cohort's LASMB004.SAV, has no wave dimension: it stays one row per respondent, without "Wave" and "Time" columns, with a message.

Which columns are wave-specific is decided per column: a column made wide by transform_lasa_data() itself is recognized by its name, or by attributes it carries where its name doesn't say enough (see Wide format); any other column is wave-specific when lasa_label_db() documents its name as a wave-specific variable – which covers LASA's irregular names too, such as t2_dat (t_dat, wave B), b_dm (dm), b2oak (oak, wave 2B), or totalalpha, which LASA's wave H file uses without a wave prefix, and a column read_lasa_sav() matched to such a name by fuzzy matching or name_corrections – or, for data that aren't long yet (no "Wave" column, or one holding nothing but the "Z" placeholder read_lasa_sav() gives a Z file and the missing values merging with that file gives – only missing values, too, in data with one row per respondent), when its name is a wave prefix followed by a variable the label database documents for that wave (the names wide format uses, see below), by any wave-specific variable it documents if the wave is 4B or L, which it doesn't document yet (lhhnch), or by a variable LASA's wave files name without a wave prefix if the wave isn't A (kseh_reden). All other columns are treated as stable, including columns the label database doesn't know. A warning names columns kept stable that look like wave-specific variables: names a merge suffixed with .x/.y, and, in wide data, variables read with their wave stripped from their name.

In long data, a column named after a variable (its long-format name) is that variable's long column, whose values stay at their rows' waves. So is a column of a wave-specific name whose values are all on rows of waves that name stands for: the waves the label database documents it at, and the wave of the LASA file the data are (as far as the data's label report lists the column) – also where the label database doesn't document the name at that wave, as for the files of waves 4B and L, which it doesn't document yet – and, for a name LASA's wave files use without a wave prefix (drinking), those undocumented waves, any wave once its values differ between a respondent's rows, and, in the data of that name's LASA file (as far as the data's label report lists the column; stacked files keep the first one's), the waves lasa_topics() lists the file at that the label database doesn't document of it yet (wave K for file 045's seh_reden), unless the file's wave-prefixed columns are wide there (a wide file joined onto other long data). In the data of a LASA file of wave L, a column the file's label report lists named l followed by a wave-specific variable (lhhnch) is that variable's long column too, so wave L's files become long as other waves' do. Wave I's immse01 to immse23 are also the long names of the migrant cohort's bimmse01 to bimmse23: such a column is the migrant cohort's long column when its values are on rows of wave MB (or its canonical_name attribute says so), and wave I's column otherwise.

Names of several waves. LASA's wave files name the baseline of every cohort (B, 2B, 3B, MB, and 4B) with the same b prefix, so a name such as blphya01 may belong to any of them, and a few other names stand for several waves too (bqvalu16 for waves 3B and J, xcancer1 for waves B and C). Each respondent's value in such a column goes to the wave the data show for that respondent: in long data, a value already on a row of one of those waves stays there; otherwise, the respondent's cohort, as far as the data (or else the respondent number) show it (the first cohort has no wave 3B, so its respondents' bqvalu16 is wave J's), and then the file the column came from (the data's "LASA_file_code" and "LASA_wave" attributes, as far as the data's label report lists the column, since a merge keeps at most the first file's attributes). If nothing says, the value goes, with a message naming the column, to the first of these waves the respondent's cohort may take part in: the wave the column's other respondents were placed at by their cohort, the wave of the data's "LASA_wave" attribute, and the column's waves in calendar order (and for a name LASA's wave files use without a wave prefix, drinking, if the respondent's cohort takes part in none of those: waves 4B and L, which the label database doesn't document yet). Such a guess doesn't count as showing the respondent's cohort, so it gives none of their rows a Time unless something else, such as their respondent number, shows the cohort (which may leave several of the column's waves open: the third cohort takes part in both of bqvalu16's) – also when the result is transformed again: the long column remembers which of its values were placed by a guess, and wide format gives those values one column, also when the guesses put them at several waves, under a name that doesn't say the wave (its original name, or else LASA's own, such as blphya01), so transforming that back guesses again, with the message. The long column keeps that memory in its attributes, which rbind(), merge(), dplyr::bind_rows(), subsetting or sorting the rows of a data frame (rather than a tibble), and writing the data to a .sav file can drop: after that, those values count as showing the cohort of the wave they were put at. To avoid guesses, transform each LASA file to long format before combining files (with format_as_long = TRUE in read_lasa_sav()).

One name stands for two variables at one wave: bmmsesc1 is file 221's mmsesc and file 421's mmsesc1 at wave MB. The data's file (or the column's canonical_name attribute) says which; otherwise it is taken as the variable the name stands for at its other waves (mmsesc1), with a message.

Merged files. data may be several LASA files merged together, in any of three shapes:

  • long (the most reliable): files read with format_as_long = TRUE, which gives each file's rows their Time while the file still shows their cohort (in a baseline file, also rows holding nothing but missing-value codes), stacked per file code with dplyr::bind_rows() (or rbind(), if the files have the same columns) and merged by respnr and "Wave" (with all = TRUE, to keep the rows of respondents missing from some files); the Time.x and Time.y columns that merge makes become one "Time" again, now also for the rows of files that didn't show the respondent's cohort on their own. Stacking and merging drop the columns' labels (or keep one file's for all rows), which transform_lasa_data() gives back (see Labels). A file without wave-specific columns (LASAZ004.SAV, LASMB004.SAV) read with format_as_long = TRUE has no "Wave" column: merge it by respnr alone;

  • wide, e.g. LASAB046.SAV, LASAC046.SAV, LASAB030.SAV, ... read with standardize = FALSE and merged by respnr (with all = TRUE), or a Z file merged with LASAZ004.SAV. merge() drops the files' attributes (dplyr's joins keep the first data set's), so the values in b columns of a respondent the data show nowhere else (one who dropped out after wave B, say) go to the baseline their respondent number says, or else are placed by a guess (see Names of several waves), which gives them no Time. So merge the baseline files of the migrant and the fourth cohort (LASMB046.SAV, LAS4B046.SAV), whose respondent numbers aren't known yet, in long format. Don't stack wide files of different cohorts that share column names (e.g. LAS2B046.SAV below LASAB046.SAV, or LASAZDC2.SAV below LASAZDC1.SAV): stack them in long format;

  • a mix: long data that wide columns were merged into by respnr, for example a Z file's – without the placeholder "Wave" column read_lasa_sav() gives a Z file, or the two "Wave" columns end up as Wave.x and Wave.y, which is an error. format = "long" moves each wide column's values to its wave's row, adding a row where a respondent has a value at a wave the long data don't have a row for yet. On those added rows, stable variables the label database documents (such as sex) are filled in from the respondent's other rows, and other columns are left missing, since they weren't measured at that wave. Merged with all = TRUE (or dplyr::full_join()), the respondents the long data lack get a row without a wave, holding the wide data's values: those of wide columns go to their waves, adding the rows they need (a row at every wave of the wide columns if there are none), and the others hold for every wave, as in wide data, so they fill each of the respondent's rows (a value in a "Time" column, or in a column of a wave-specific variable the label database documents, needs a wave, so it is an error). Where no wide columns were merged in, such respondents have no row in long format (with a message), but one in wide format.

Wide format has one row per respondent and drops the "Wave" and "Time" columns. Each wave-specific variable gets one column per wave at which it has any value, and a long column made from wide columns gets all of those columns back, also ones without any value. With prefix = "Wave", a column's name is its wave's lowercase LASA prefix followed by the variable name: boak, coak, doak, ... Waves 2B, 3B, 4B, and MB get the prefixes b2, b3, b4, and mb (as LASA's own zoa2/zoa3 files do for 2B and 3B), so they don't collide with wave B's columns. Where LASA's own name for the variable at that wave stands for nothing else, the column gets that name instead (m15wrth is bm15twtrh at wave B and c15wtrth at wave C; totalalpha, wave H's name without a wave prefix, stays totalalpha). A column that came from a wide LASA file gets its original name back (e.g. t2_dat rather than bt_dat), unless its values went to several waves or the name doesn't say its wave by itself: the b_dm column of LASAZDC2.SAV, which holds the second cohort's baseline, becomes b2dm.

With prefix = "Time", names are t, the "Time", and an underscore followed by the variable name: t0_oak holds each respondent's value at their own baseline, t1_oak at their cohort's next wave (wave C for the first cohort, F for the second), and so on, so the cohorts share columns. A cohort column after respnr gives each respondent's cohort, which transforming the data back to long format uses. It is LASA's cohort variable the way read_lasa_sav() reads LASAZ002.SAV's – a factor of its value labels ("cohort 1 (1992)", "cohort 2 (2002)", "cohort 3 (2012)"), with its labels – so the result merges with that file by respnr and cohort, read with to_factor = TRUE (the default); read with to_factor = FALSE, merge it by respnr alone (the cohort.x and cohort.y columns that gives are combined, see above). The fourth cohort, whose code 4 the label database doesn't document yet, gets the level "4", as read_lasa_sav() reads that code, and the migrant cohort, which LASAZ002.SAV doesn't have, the level "migrant cohort" after it. These levels come where the data have respondents of these cohorts – "4" also with only the migrant cohort's – so that each cohort keeps its code (1 to 5) when the factor becomes numbers (in a .sav file, say). The column replaces a cohort column data have, which must then be LASA's: any other column named cohort (in any capitalization) is an error, so rename it first. Wave A, which has no Time, keeps its own column (aoak). Every other value needs a Time: values at a wave without one for their respondent are an error, except missing-value codes, which are left out with a message. A respondent whose rows have a Time while the data leave their cohort open (rows of waves I to L only, which the third and the migrant cohort give the same Time, of a respondent whose number doesn't say the cohort, or says one the data rule out) gets a missing cohort, with a warning: their columns can't be transformed back, also not by their respondent number. A column holding several cohorts' waves (t0_oak: B, 2B, ...) gets those waves' types, value labels and user-missing codes, combined the way long format combines waves, with a warning where their user-missing codes don't combine, and their "wave_label"/"labels_wave" as one entry per wave. Original names aren't kept with prefix = "Time", also not when such data are made wide again with prefix = "Wave".

A column stays stable in wide format when it has a single value per respondent and isn't a documented wave-specific variable; a documented stable variable (such as sex) only needs to agree across the rows where it isn't missing. A wide column whose name still doesn't say which wave and variable it holds (a name the label database doesn't document, or a wave B name the later cohorts' baselines share, such as blphya01, and, in a result with wave 4B, whose files use the baselines' b names, any baseline's b name) carries the attributes "LASA_wave" and "LASA_long_name", which transforming it back uses, also without the result's other columns. Base R's merge() and row subsetting drop those attributes from factor and numeric columns (haven's labelled columns keep them); the column is then placed like a column of LASA's own files, see Names of several waves.

Labels travel with the data. A long column keeps each wave's own "wave_label"/"labels_wave" as one entry per wave. Its variable label is the one its waves share, or else their harmonized (cross-wave) label, or else the first wave's. Its value labels are those of all waves combined; if a code is labelled differently at different waves, it gets the harmonized value labels, or none. SPSS user-missing codes ("na_values", "na_range") are combined as long as that marks exactly the same values missing on every wave's rows; otherwise the long column gets none, with a warning. Factor levels are combined across waves; wave-specific columns whose types don't combine (e.g. a factor at one wave and numbers at another) become text, without value labels or user-missing codes, with a warning. Time spans (difftime) get a unit every wave's values convert to exactly, the first wave's if possible; date-times that become text are written in UTC ("2021-10-31 00:30:00+0000"), so they read back as the same moment. Converting back to wide restores each wide column's original type (also from text), attributes, and user-missing codes, as long as its values still fit them.

In long data, the column of a wave-specific variable the label database documents that has lost its labels – rbind(), dplyr::bind_rows() and merge() drop them from factor and numeric columns, and rbind() keeps one file's for all rows of labelled columns – gets back the labels read_lasa_sav() gives the variable at each wave it has values at, from the label database: "wave_label"/"labels_wave" with an entry per wave, "canonical_name", the harmonized label and value labels where the database has them, and as "label" and "labels" the harmonized ones, or else the waves' shared (or first) wording and all their value labels. The data then get a "variable.labels" attribute too, if they had none. So does a long column made of wide columns that have all lost their labels (wide files merged with merge()); wide format gives those columns back as they were. Labels of a column's own (not ones the database gives the variable, such as a user's own wording) are kept as they are, and a column with "wave_label" entries for some of its waves only gets the other waves', as long as those it has are the database's. A wave at which the database documents the variable with different labels in several files (partner at wave MB) gets none.

See also

read_lasa_sav() (format_as_long), apply_lasa_labels(), lasa_label_db()

Examples

# A Z-file-shaped data frame: knee osteoarthritis (oak) of two
# respondents of the first cohort (waves B, C, and F) and one of the
# second (waves 2B and F), plus a stable variable (sex).
wide <- data.frame(
  respnr = c(101, 102, 201),
  sex = c(1, 2, 2),
  boak = c(0, 2, NA),
  coak = c(1, 8, NA),
  b2oak = c(NA, NA, 1),
  foak = c(2, NA, 0)
)

# format = "long" is the default. Time counts the waves since each
# respondent's own baseline: wave F is Time 4 for the first cohort, but
# Time 1 for the second.
long <- transform_lasa_data(wide)
long
#>   respnr Wave Time sex oak
#> 1    101    B    0   1   0
#> 2    101    C    1   1   1
#> 3    101    F    4   1   2
#> 4    102    B    0   2   2
#> 5    102    C    1   2   8
#> 6    201   2B    0   2   1
#> 7    201    F    1   2   0

# And back again, with wave letters or Time numbers as prefixes:
transform_lasa_data(long, format = "wide")
#>   respnr sex boak coak b2oak foak
#> 1    101   1    0    1    NA    2
#> 2    102   2    2    8    NA   NA
#> 3    201   2   NA   NA     1    0
transform_lasa_data(long, format = "wide", prefix = "Time")
#>   respnr          cohort sex t0_oak t1_oak t4_oak
#> 1    101 cohort 1 (1992)   1      0      1      2
#> 2    102 cohort 1 (1992)   2      2      8     NA
#> 3    201 cohort 2 (2002)   2      1      0     NA

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
# Read a Z file straight into long format:
oa <- read_lasa_sav("LASAZOA1.SAV", format_as_long = TRUE)
} # }
